newsitem.title: CANADA: American strike to have minimal cargo impact.
newsitem.headline: American strike to have minimal cargo impact.

text.p: A threatened strike by American Airlines pilots might be more than a minor inconvience for the U.S. Postal Service and South American produce shippers, but should not cause too many problems for the rest of the air freight industry, said U.S. analysts.
American's pilots are threatening to go on strike from midnight on Friday if Federal mediation talks fail to settle their contract dispute.
"If there is going to be an American Airlines strike, it is certainly going to be a passenger story, not a cargo story," says Greg Smith, analyst with the Colography Group in Marietta, Georgia.
This is air cargo's low season, and American's rivals have enough space on most domestic and international corridors to accommodate American's traffic, he said.

Initially, there could be a few exceptions, notably some U.S.-Latin American corridors where capacity is governed by restrictive bilateral air treaties, such as northbound from Lima and Bogota or U.S.-Brazil routes in both directions, he said.

American operates about 40 percent of the frequencies from Miami to South America, says Ned Laird, head of the Seattle-based Air Cargo Management Group. Southbound to Brazil is a tight market right now. Also, shippers of Chilean produce and seafoods may face some space problems next week if there is a strike, he said.

"There is (other) capacity available this time of year, but it's going to be indirect for some shippers," added Laird. "There will be rerouting of some Brazilian freight through the west coast of South America, to get it to Rio, Sao Paolo and Manaus.

That view is echoed by Colography's Smith. "If there is going to be an impact in cargo, it will be internationally in the Central America/South America region, although again, in reality, I think there is plenty of lift."

San Juan, Puerto Rico, is another American hub and potential bottleneck in the early days of a strike, but it is dominated by a small number of large accounts - electronics manufacturers, apparel makers and pharmaceutical companies - "and it would be very easy to put together a couple of big charters," said Smith.

To show how fortunate the timing of the strike is for shippers, a week earlier and a walkout would have crippled South American flower imports for Valentine's Day on Friday, says Brian Clancy, a principal with the MergeGlobal consultancy in Arlington, Va.

Domestically, scheduled carriers like American long ago lost the overnight component of the freight market to integrators like Federal Express Corp and Uunited Parcel Service of America and heavy freight specialists like Emery Worldwide. The second or third day freight they carry can shift over to truck, said Colography's Smith. "So by and large, it's a real non-event domestically."
The biggest impact of a strike might be to force up pricing short term, say the analysts.

"American is notorious for being an aggressive spot pricer," said MergeGlobal's Clancy. "So in effect (what a strike would do) is take a relatively reliable cheap source of lift off the market which means the forwarders have to realign how they flow the traffic.
Forwarders which ship predominantly with American and don't have contracts or volume discounts with other carriers "are going to have to pay ... the prix du jour (spot rates)," said ACMG's Laird.

By law, the U.S. Postal Service must use scheduled airlines, not integrated carriers, for most air mail traffic, and it might have to reroute traffic around big American hubs like Chicago or Dallas to cope with a shortage of alternate lift at those airports.
"Basically what it means is that a lot of postal transportation managers aren't going to be getting a lot of sleep over the next few weeks," said Clancy.
About 40 percent of American's domestic tonnage is mail. Second tier carriers like ValuJet and Kiwi Air might pick up some mail business, said ACMG's Laird.
Nor, say the analysts, would a strike seriously inconvenience importers or exporters in markets like Dallas. A great deal of their freight already comes by road from gateways like Los Angeles.
